# Product of Everything Else — Explained, One Approach at a Time

<!-- Generated by scripts/gen-explained.mjs from src/data/problems/arrays-hashing/product-except-self.ts.
     Edit the data, then run `npm run docs:explained`. Edits here are overwritten. -->

**Arrays & Hashing** · medium · [the same question on LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/product-of-array-except-self/)

Given an integer array, return an array where each position holds the product of every element except the one at that position. Solve it without using division, in linear time.

## What the input promises

- 2 <= nums.length <= 10^5
- -30 <= nums[i] <= 30
- every answer is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer
- division is off the table — which matters most precisely because the array may contain zeros

## Examples

| Input | Output | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]` | `[24, 12, 8, 6]` | — |
| `nums = [-1, 1, 0, -3, 3]` | `[0, 0, 9, 0, 0]` | A single zero makes every other answer zero. |

<details>
<summary>Hints, one nudge at a time — open them in order</summary>

1. The answer at i is (everything to the left of i) × (everything to the right of i). Two independent questions.
2. Both halves can be built by a running product — one sweep left to right, one right to left.
3. You do not need to store both: write the left products into the output, then multiply the right products in on a second sweep.

</details>

---

## 1. Product of the others, each time

For every index, loop over the whole array multiplying together every element except the one at that index.

```python
def product_except_self(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    out = []
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        product = 1
        for j in range(len(nums)):
            if j != i:
                product *= nums[j]
        out.append(product)
    return out
```

**O(n²) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] productExceptSelf(int[] nums) {
    int n = nums.length;
    int[] out = new int[n];
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        int prod = 1;
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
            if (j != i) prod *= nums[j];
        }
        out[i] = prod;
    }
    return out;
}
```

</details>

<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    vector<int> out(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        int prod = 1;
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
            if (j != i) prod *= nums[j];
        }
        out[i] = prod;
    }
    return out;
}
```

## 2. Two prefix arrays

> **Why now.** The nested loop recomputes the same partial products for every index. Storing each running product once makes the whole thing linear — at the cost of two extra arrays that are each read exactly once.

Build one array of running products from the left and another from the right, then multiply them position by position.

```python
def product_except_self(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    left = [1] * n
    right = [1] * n
    for i in range(1, n):
        left[i] = left[i - 1] * nums[i - 1]
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
        right[i] = right[i + 1] * nums[i + 1]
    return [left[i] * right[i] for i in range(n)]
```

**O(n) time · O(n) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] productExceptSelf(int[] nums) {
    int n = nums.length;
    int[] left = new int[n];
    int[] right = new int[n];
    Arrays.fill(left, 1);
    Arrays.fill(right, 1);
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        left[i] = left[i - 1] * nums[i - 1];
    }
    for (int i = n - 2; i >= 0; i--) {
        right[i] = right[i + 1] * nums[i + 1];
    }
    int[] result = new int[n];
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        result[i] = left[i] * right[i];
    }
    return result;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> productExceptSelf(const vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    vector<int> left(n, 1);
    vector<int> right(n, 1);
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        left[i] = left[i - 1] * nums[i - 1];
    }
    for (int i = n - 2; i >= 0; i--) {
        right[i] = right[i + 1] * nums[i + 1];
    }
    vector<int> result(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        result[i] = left[i] * right[i];
    }
    return result;
}
```

</details>

## 3. The one to remember

> **Why now.** Holding the two prefix arrays makes the idea obvious but keeps 2n numbers alive to read each of them exactly once. The output array can carry the left products while the right sweep folds its running product straight into them, so the same two passes need no storage beyond the answer.

Sweep left to right writing into the output the product of everything strictly before each index, carrying a running product. Then sweep right to left with a second running product of everything strictly after, multiplying it into what is already there. Each position ends up holding left × right, which is every element but its own. Nothing is ever divided, so a zero — or two — behaves like any other value rather than being a special case.

```python
def product_except_self(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    out = [1] * n
    running = 1
    for i in range(n):
        out[i] = running
        running *= nums[i]
    running = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        out[i] *= running
        running *= nums[i]
    return out
```

**O(n) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] productExceptSelf(int[] nums) {

    int running = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        out[i] = running;
        running *= nums[i];
    }
    running = 1;
    for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        out[i] *= running;
        running *= nums[i];
    }
    return out;
}
```

</details>

```cpp
    }

}
```

## The arc

| # | Approach | Cost | What it adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Product of the others, each time | O(n²) time · O(1) space | the baseline — nothing before it |
| 2 | Two prefix arrays | O(n) time · O(n) space | The nested loop recomputes the same partial products for every index. Storing each running product once makes the whole thing linear — at the cost of two extra arrays that are each read exactly once. |
| 3 | The one to remember | O(n) time · O(1) space | Holding the two prefix arrays makes the idea obvious but keeps 2n numbers alive to read each of them exactly once. The output array can carry the left products while the right sweep folds its running product straight into them, so the same two passes need no storage beyond the answer. |

## Full runnable script

Every rung in one file, printed against the inputs `npm run verify:run`
drives the Java and C++ blocks with. Run it: `python explained.py`.

```python
def product_except_self_product_of_the_others_each_time(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    out = []
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        product = 1
        for j in range(len(nums)):
            if j != i:
                product *= nums[j]
        out.append(product)
    return out


def product_except_self_two_prefix_arrays(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    left = [1] * n
    right = [1] * n
    for i in range(1, n):
        left[i] = left[i - 1] * nums[i - 1]
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
        right[i] = right[i + 1] * nums[i + 1]
    return [left[i] * right[i] for i in range(n)]


def product_except_self_the_one_to_remember(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    out = [1] * n
    running = 1
    for i in range(n):
        out[i] = running
        running *= nums[i]
    running = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        out[i] *= running
        running *= nums[i]
    return out

APPROACHES = [
    product_except_self_product_of_the_others_each_time,
    product_except_self_two_prefix_arrays,
    product_except_self_the_one_to_remember,
]

# the same inputs npm run verify:run drives the Java and C++ blocks with:
# the zero, which is why division is banned — one zero ([-1,1,0,-3,3]) and two ([0,0,4])
CASES = [
    lambda: ([1,2,3,4],),
    lambda: ([-1,1,0,-3,3],),
    lambda: ([2,3],),
    lambda: ([0,0,4],),
    lambda: ([-2,-3,-4],),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for fn in APPROACHES:
        answers = []
        for make in CASES:
            try:
                answers.append(fn(*make()))
            except BaseException as exc:  # a rung that raises names itself
                answers.append(f"!{exc}")
        print(f"{fn.__name__:<53} -> {answers}")
```
